blocks.text: 2 John is a compact letter: it opens with sender and addressee, offers a blessing, addresses its central concern, anticipates a visit, and closes with greetings. Its repeated themes are truth, love, obedience, and the danger posed by deceivers. Love is not treated as sentiment alone; the letter defines it as walking according to God’s commandments.

The sender calls himself “the elder,” which is a role rather than a personal name. The “elect lady and her children” may refer to an individual woman, a household, a congregation, or a personified community; the closing reference to an “elect sister” does not settle the question. The letter therefore leaves the precise identities of both sender and recipients open.

“Truth” is more than correct information in this letter. It is presented as abiding with the community, as the setting of the elder’s love, and as a way of life: some of the addressee’s children are praised for “walking in truth.” That walking is described as conduct shaped by the command received from the Father, while love is defined as walking in that commandment.

The letter’s warning focuses on people who do not confess Jesus Christ “coming in the flesh”; it calls such a figure “the deceiver and the antichrist.” The exact force of “coming in flesh” and the identity of the opponents remain debated, so labels for a particular later movement go beyond what this short letter itself demonstrates. The warning should be read as the letter’s compressed boundary-setting language, not as a basis for speculation about unnamed groups.

The instruction not to receive a teacher into “your house” or offer a greeting concerns more than private politeness. In ancient travel, hospitality could include lodging, food, meeting space, patronage, and public endorsement, though the precise combination intended here is uncertain. The letter links welcome to participation in a teacher’s work, so its concern is material and public complicity; the meanings of “house” and “greeting” themselves remain open to more than one interpretation.

The final verses make clear that this written note is not meant to say everything. “Paper and ink” are ordinary writing materials, and the elder hopes instead for direct, face-to-face conversation so that joy may be complete. The closing greeting preserves the letter’s relational character while leaving the exact identity of the “elect sister” unresolved.

sections.title: A Letter Meant to Be Completed in Person
